title: Chapter 9
paragraphs: "Oblonsky's carriage!" the porter shouted in a gruff bass. The carriage pulled up and both men got in. It was only for the first few moments, as the carriage rolled out of the clubhouse gates, that Levin was still under the spell of the club—the air of rest, comfort, and impeccable form. But as soon as the carriage hit the street and he felt it jolt over the uneven road, heard the angry shout of a sledge driver coming the other way, and saw in the half-light the red blind of a tavern and the shop windows, the spell broke, and he began to turn over what he'd done and wonder whether he was right to be going to see Anna. What would Kitty say? But Stepan Arkadyevitch gave him no time to think, and as if reading his doubts, swept them aside.

"How glad I am," he said, "that you're going to know her! Dolly has wanted this for ages. And Lvov has been to see her, and goes often. She may be my sister," Stepan Arkadyevitch went on, "but I'll say it anyway—she's a remarkable woman. You'll see. Her situation is very painful, especially right now."

"We're negotiating with her husband about a divorce. He's agreed; but there are complications about the boy, and the whole thing—which should have been settled long ago—has dragged on for three months now. As soon as the divorce is through, she'll marry Vronsky. How stupid these old ceremonies are, that nobody believes in and that only get in the way of people being happy!" Stepan Arkadyevitch put in. "Anyway, once it's done, their position will be as regular as mine, as yours."

"Oh, it's a long and tiresome story! The whole business is in such an awkward place here. The point is, she's been in Moscow for three months, where everyone knows her, waiting for the divorce; she goes out nowhere, sees no woman except Dolly, because, you understand, she doesn't want people coming as a favor. Even that fool Princess Varvara has dropped her, considering it a breach of propriety. Now, you see, any other woman in her position wouldn't have managed. But you'll see how she has arranged her life—how calm, how dignified she is. Left, in the crescent across from the church!" Stepan Arkadyevitch shouted, leaning out of the window. "Phew! it's hot!" he said, despite the twelve degrees of frost, throwing his already-open overcoat even wider.
"But she has a daughter—surely she's busy looking after her?" said Levin.

"I think you picture every woman simply as a female, _une couveuse_," said Stepan Arkadyevitch. "If she's occupied, it has to be with children. No—she's bringing her up well, I believe, but you don't hear about it. She's busy, first of all, with what she's writing. I see you're smiling skeptically, but you shouldn't be. She's writing a children's book, and never says a word about it to anyone, but she read it to me and I gave the manuscript to Vorkuev ... you know the publisher ... he's an author himself, I think. He understands these things, and he says it's a remarkable piece of work. But are you imagining she's some authoress?—not a bit of it. She's a woman with a heart, before anything else, but you'll see. Right now she has a little English girl living with her, and a whole family she's looking after."

"Why must you take everything in the worst sense? It's not philanthropy, it's from the heart. They—meaning Vronsky—had a trainer, an Englishman, first-rate at his job, but a drunk. He's completely lost to drink—delirium tremens—and his family was left destitute. She saw them, helped them, got more and more involved, and now the whole family is on her hands. And not as patronage, you know, throwing money at it; she's coaching the boys herself in Russian to prepare them for the high school, and she's taken the little girl in to live with her. But you'll see for yourself."
The carriage pulled into the courtyard, and Stepan Arkadyevitch rang loudly at the entrance, where several sledges were standing.

And without bothering to ask the servant who opened the door whether the lady was at home, Stepan Arkadyevitch walked straight into the hall. Levin followed, more and more uncertain whether he was doing the right thing or the wrong one.

Glancing at himself in the glass, Levin noticed his face was flushed, but he was sure he wasn't drunk, and he followed Stepan Arkadyevitch up the carpeted stairs. At the top, Stepan Arkadyevitch asked the footman, who bowed to him like a close friend, who was with Anna Arkadyevna, and got the answer: M. Vorkuev.

Walking through the dining-room—a smallish room with dark, paneled walls—Stepan Arkadyevitch and Levin crossed the soft carpet to the half-dark study, lit only by a single lamp with a big dark shade. Another lamp with a reflector was mounted on the wall, lighting up a large full-length portrait of a woman that Levin couldn't help looking at. It was the portrait of Anna, painted in Italy by Mihailov. While Stepan Arkadyevitch went past the _treillage_, and the male voice that had been speaking fell silent, Levin stood gazing at the portrait, which seemed to step out of its frame in the bright light thrown on it, and he could not pull himself away. He literally forgot where he was, and didn't even hear what was being said—he could not take his eyes off the marvelous portrait. It was not a picture but a living, beautiful woman, with dark curling hair, with bare arms and shoulders, with a thoughtful smile on lips covered with soft down; triumphantly and gently she looked at him with eyes that left him at a loss. She wasn't living only because she was more beautiful than any living woman can be.

"I'm delighted!" he heard a voice suddenly say close to him—clearly addressed to him, the voice of the very woman he had just been admiring in the portrait. Anna had come out from behind the _treillage_ to greet him, and in the dim light of the study Levin saw the very woman of the portrait, in a dark-blue shot dress, not in the same pose or with the same expression, but with the same beauty the artist had caught. She was less dazzling in real life, but on the other hand there was something fresh and alluring in the living woman that was not in the portrait.
